Tech stocks aren't lacking in growth stories for 2027. The problem is that smart money is increasingly selective about which companies it's willing to pay a premium for. AI is still the big story, but skepticism is growing about whether the money invested will deliver the promised returns.

You could see that shift very clearly in the Bank of America fund manager survey for November. Investors were clearly pulling back from tech at the fastest rate since June 2006 (their net overweight position in tech fell from 37% in October to just 12%). Even more telling is that 38% of the 169 managers surveyed (who in total manage $461 billion) believe that firms are over-investing in AI and over half (52%) expect at least one of the major AI players to reduce its capital expenditure over the next 6 months.

The concerns led to a wider sell-off. The Nasdaq 100 Index is down over 10% in the second half of 2026. Semiconductors were particularly hard hit as investors have re-priced AI companies and rethought the sustainability of data center spending. This wasn't necessarily a rejection of AI per se. It was more a case of investors questioning how much expected growth had already been priced in.

There's still a lot of money flowing into the sector. JPMorgan expects AI-related capex to be $1.4tn in 2027, almost double its 2026 estimate. A significant portion will go into data centers, servers, networking gear and advanced semiconductors. For a closer look at where this spending is going, see our breakdown of the eight companies Morgan Stanley expects to spend $1.6 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027. JPMorgan does, however, expect spending growth to tail off significantly from 2028.

The wider tech sector isn't moving in the same direction. Chip and data center suppliers are clearly on the up because of AI spending. On the other hand, the software and cloud businesses have to prove that their customers are actually going to spend more. For investors, it's all about separating the wheat from the chaff. Some businesses have sustainable demand while others are just in the midst of a spending spike.

The search for value is also playing out across the broader market. In a recent article, we look at 10 dirt-cheap stocks positioned to soar in 2027, focusing on companies that trade at attractive valuations despite strong expected revenue growth.

So, what are the best tech stocks to buy for 2027? You can find the expanded list of 10 Best Tech Stocks to Buy for 2027 According to Hedge Funds. We discussed the top 5 stocks below.

title: Caterpillar is quietly making plans for a bigger 2027
detail:
Caterpillar is quietly making plans for a bigger 2027
Peace Longe, Celine Provini
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 11:47 AM PST 4 min read
CAT
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you visit construction sites often, there's a high chance you've seen Caterpillar's yellow machines before.

These machines help to dig the foundations of new homes and warehouses. They also clear highways for road crews and remove dirt from where new neighborhoods are rising.

In the past few days, Caterpillar (CAT) shares have been having a tough run. The stock closed at $570.49 on Nov. 16, and it is down by about 8% so far this month.

However, the company is already preparing for 2027. And based on its preparations, one Wall Street analyst believes investors are overlooking a key part of the business.

Why Bank of America thinks the market is misreading Caterpillar stock

Caterpillar recently hosted its Compact Construction event for investors. At the event, the company discussed their plans for 2027. Some Wall Street analysts were present at the time.

Bank of America's Michael Feniger, a senior analyst who covers Caterpillar and other heavy equipment makers, kept his Buy rating on the stock and a $746 price target after attending the event, Benzinga reported.

Also read: Warren Buffett makes another massive $5.47 billion move

That price target is about 31% above CAT's current share price. In his note, Feniger said the market "is applying a discount to CAT's Machinery Construction unit."

He pointed to a recent joint venture between rival companies CNH Industrial and Kobelco as proof that construction equipment makers are worth more than Caterpillar's stock price suggests. The joint venture of those two companies is valued at roughly 10 times EBITDA.

Caterpillar equipment at a construction site in Lafayette, California.neiu20001 / Getty Images
How Caterpillar makes its money, and what Q3 2026 told us

Caterpillar builds and sells excavators, dozers, haul trucks, gas turbines, and other heavy equipment. The company also makes the engines inside these heavy machines. In addition, Caterpillar lends money to the contractors who buy its equipment through Cat Financial.

Even though the stock has been down in the past few days, Caterpillar reported a strong third quarter in 2026. The company reported that revenue hit $20.68 billion. That's up 17% from the same quarter last year.

Caterpillar's adjusted profit per share also jumped to $7.20 from $4.95. CEO Joe Creed said the results "reflect the durability of our end markets, with strong order rates and a record backlog."

Related: Berkshire Hathaway earnings expose unexpected problem beneath strong economy

The stock dropped even though CAT beat expectations because Wall Street focused on a cautious Q4 outlook. However, I think that reaction was a little overblown, and Feniger agrees.

His team sees Caterpillar's earnings per share of $26.75 in 2026 rising to $33.50 in 2027. They also expect that number to rise to $42 by 2028.

What a $4.2 billion Nevada project and Texas permits mean for investors

Caterpillar recently won an equipment contract tied to a $4.2 billion project in Nevada. And its dealers are building out rental fleets to bid on similar jobs.

More Construction Stocks:

Berkshire almost doubles stake in tumbling housing stock

Morgan Stanley sees Caterpillar rental gains, stays cautious

Micron freezes Taiwan plant as workers demand bigger cut

Also, according to the Texas Tribune, state regulators have resumed the process of reviewing permits for data centers after Governor Greg Abbott paused them earlier this year.

Based on that, SpaceX received a permit to run 750 megawatts of gas turbines in Cameron County, Politico reported. The setup includes 18 units made by Caterpillar's Solar Turbines.

Data centers need both buildings and reliable electricity to run well, and Caterpillar sells both.

What still needs to go right for Caterpillar stock

Even though Bank of America thinks CAT is underpriced, not every analyst agrees. D.A. Davidson recently cut its price target on CAT to $685 from $882 while keeping a Neutral rating, Investing.com reported. The firm cited concerns about the company's valuation, even as all three business segments grew.

Feniger described the company as being "in growth mode" for the next few years. That's why he admitted that there are still risks involved. Dealers are expanding their fleets at a time when the construction outlook is still unclear. Especially with the high interest rates and political uncertainty following the November midterms.

However, even with the risks BofA thinks Caterpillar's 2027 plans look credible. For the stock to recover, construction demand needs to hold up, data center buildouts need to continue, and dealers need to hit the fleet targets they have shared.

title: BofA Sees S&P 500 Rising 8% in 2027: Are Your ETFs Ready for a Soft Landing?
detail:
BofA Sees S&P 500 Rising 8% in 2027: Are Your ETFs Ready for a Soft Landing?
Aparajita Dutta

^GSPC
SPY
VFFSX
IVV

Bank of America has just delivered a forecast that is equal parts reassuring and sobering. Savita Subramanian, the bank's head of U.S. equity strategy, expects the S&P 500 Index to close 2027 at 7,800 — a roughly 8.3% upside from the index's late-November close near 7,200. 

For S&P 500 ETF investors, a projected 8% gain in 2027 offers some encouragement after a volatile 2026. Yet, BofA's target carries an uncomfortable caveat. That 7,800 level is not a new territory. 

The S&P 500 first touched it in October before a series of November shocks dragged the index down by more than 11%. In other words, BofA is not forecasting a breakout. It is predicting a round trip. 

The 8% gain simply reflects how far the market has fallen, not a sudden burst of optimism from the strategist who first set this target in September when it implied only 2% upside. 

For ETF investors, that distinction matters enormously. Why? Because recovering lost ground carries a very different risk-reward profile than hitting new highs. Because of this, passive investors have to ask if broad index funds can still deliver strong returns without runaway momentum.

Even so, for long-term investors looking to capture a steady recovery without gambling on single-stock winners, low-cost S&P 500 ETFs remain the default vehicle. Before identifying the standout funds, however, it is worth digging deeper into the factors expected to keep the index buoyant — though not dramatically higher — through 2027.

What Could Drive the S&P 500 in 2027?

BofA's caution stems from a supply-and-demand problem that has been building beneath the surface. 

Subramanian flags a worsening balance: share issuance and IPOs are rising, while corporate buybacks, which have been a reliable source of demand for equities for long, are fading. She also warned that an aging population could lead to retirement fund outflows, adding pressure to an S&P 500 already trading at elevated valuations.

In addition to that, fading earnings and margin visibility, lingering questions about whether the AI investment cycle will actually pay off, and a recent bout of "just buy the index" complacency have made the downside risks hard to ignore.

Maybe that's why the range of estimates is also wide. BofA's bull case envisions 8,500, while its bear case sits at 6,600, which is not a very narrow corridor. 
Still, clear tailwinds are expected to keep the index buoyant, which are likely to have convinced other major Wall Street houses to set far higher targets.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both set 2027 targets of 8,700, while Deutsche Bank projects 9,000 and JPMorgan expects 8,200.

Major U.S. banks are changing the rules around what can happen inside Americans' accounts — and customers could be the ones left paying the price.

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon sounded the alarm during the bank's third-quarter earnings call, warning that outside tools could create an entirely new class of threat.

Top Picks

Can you hold physical gold in your retirement account? Yes. Get Goldco's Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"You don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them," he said (1).

And if customers authorize those agents to act on their behalf, Dimon warned that the consequences may no longer fall on the bank.

"If people are using them, they should understand the risk. There's a liability transfer," he said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer."

The "rogue agents" worrying America's biggest bank are third-party AI tools designed to take action on a user's behalf.

Unlike conventional chatbots that simply answer questions, AI agents can analyze spending, search for better returns, pay bills or potentially move money between accounts. But if one misunderstands an instruction, exceeds its authority or exposes a customer's credentials, the customer could be left responsible for what happens next.

JPMorgan formalized its position in an updated Digital Services Agreement (2) that took effect Oct. 27. The bank now prohibits third parties — including outside AI, automated tools and data aggregators — from using a customer's login credentials to enter its digital platforms.

If a customer nevertheless permits that access, JPMorgan says it can treat the third party's actions and instructions as authorized — even when they are inaccurate, unintended or inconsistent with what the customer actually requested.

Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) delivered a similar warning directly to customers.

"Never share your user ID or password with another person or an outside service, including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf," the bank advised (3).

"If you do share your user ID and password," it added, "keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access."

Bank of America issues blunt 2027 hard-landing warning on S&P 500

Judging from Wall Street's early 2027 stock market forecasts, it might seem that autumn's turbulence was more or less a brief speed bump. 

Major investment banks still continue to project another banner year ahead, even after Federal Reserve rate-hike jitters and AI spending doubts knocked the S&P 500 down from its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93 to 7,201.09 on Nov. 24.

Bank of America Securities isn't buying that complacency though. In a note shared with me, Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett issued a blunt reality check for investors heading into 2027.

Though most on Wall Street are calling for smooth sailing, Hartnett warns that a painful economic slowdown is perhaps the single biggest underpriced risk in markets today and is advising clients to play defense now.

Bank of America outlines a possible S&P 500 decline amid recession risks.
Spencer Platt / Getty Images
Inside Bank of America's 2027 S&P 500 forecast and hard-landing math

Hartnett's alarm starts off with a growing gap between market nerves and institutional positioning. 

As per Bank of America's November Global Fund Manager Survey as reported by Biggo, just 3% of fund managers are forecasting a steep downturn over the next 12 months, in comparison with 50% expecting a soft landing and 42% predicting no landing at all.

More Wall Street:

Arista Networks stock gets fresh backing from Jim Cramer and Wall Street

Oracle stock sinks as Wall Street confronts a $20 billion AI problem

Wall Street just got a candid look at who is winning the AI race

Cash levels have dropped to a historically thin 3.6%, down from 3.9% in October, even as global stock funds absorbed $310 billion over the past four weeks.

That crowding leaves stocks remarkably exposed. Hartnett warned that a "hard landing" is the biggest threat to market consensus, arguing that Wall Street projections of 15% to 20% global earnings growth are currently looking too optimistic as AI capital spending and K-shaped wealth effects taper off. 

In a true bust, he projects a bear market that drags the S&P 500 down to nearly 6,666, implying a 7.4% to 8% downside from late-November levels.

For clarity, recession isn't Bank of America's base case. 

Under a "Goldilocks" soft landing scenario that involves global growth above 3%, dropping inflation, sliding oil prices, and 21 global rate cuts in the back half of 2027, Hartnett expects a bull market to broaden out that could potentially carry the S&P 500 to around 7,777, an 8% increase from Nov. 24, yielding 4% to 8% upside for global stocks, with an extreme AI-boom surprise reaching 8,888.

That discipline echoes Bank of America's broader view.

I've learned that a stock can deliver impressive results and still struggle to move higher. Sometimes, the market is less interested in what a company has just achieved than in whether it can keep delivering at the same pace.

Dell Technologies (DELL) reported a record third quarter on Nov. 24, raised guidance, and still fell about 5% in early trading the following day. 

Seven of the eight firms that updated price targets lowered them, according to TheFly. Bank of America's Wamsi Mohan, ranked 26th out of 12,606 analysts on TipRanks with a 59% success rate, cut his target to $500 from $600 in a note shared with TheStreet, a 16.67% reduction.

His reasoning? "The market continues to question sustainability."

DELL is still up 129.34% year to date and 129.27% over one year as of Nov. 25, according to Yahoo Finance. This is despite recording an all-time high of $595.51 on Sept. 18, 2026, and currently trading 52% below the high.

The stock is not struggling. The question is how much growth is already in the price.

Also Read: Dell Technologies Q3 2027 Earnings: Recap of $DELL Earnings Call, Stock Forecast

Dell's tension: a great quarter, a lower multiple

Mohan said Dell delivered another strong quarter and outlook. What he changed was the valuation multiple he applies to Dell's earnings, citing risks to the AI infrastructure buildout and Dell's exposure to neoclouds. These newer AI-focused cloud providers have leaned heavily on debt to expand.

That worry has a backdrop. Piper Sandler pointed to the "sharp sell-off across AI and infrastructure names over the last two months, according to Stocktwits." 

More Tech:

Apple CEO signals surprising change for iPhone users

Comcast sends wake-up call to employees as customers cut services

AI agents' growing role in payments raises an awkward question

I covered the same fear when Oracle's credit spreads widened, and its bonds were questioned. The debate has moved from whether AI demand is real to who is financing it, and for how long.

Dell's answer came from COO Jeff Clarke on the earnings call: "We've had no customers reschedule business. The backlog continues to be very firm." He said the company remains "highly selective" with Neocloud customers and that every order is "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power."

What the Dell quarter showed

According to Dell's earnings release, Q3 revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Non-GAAP EPS was $9.45, up 265%. Cash flow from operations was a record $4.5 billion for a third quarter.

Canadian banks have little room for earnings disappointments at premium valuations, Bank of America said as it trimmed fourth-quarter earnings per share estimates.

Bank of America expects management updates to do little to change investor optimism, with investors watching for early signs of a pickup in domestic investment.

Canadian banks trade at 13.8 times estimated 2027 earnings, while Bank of America forecasts earnings per share growth of 10.8% in 2027, down from 19.4% in fiscal year 2026.

With earnings growth set to slow, the bank expects revisions to earnings estimates to be the main driver of share performance.

Bank of America cited slower capital markets activity, expected restructuring charges at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) (TSX:CM) and Royal Bank of Canada (TSX:RY), and higher credit costs, particularly at Bank of Nova Scotia (TSX:BNS), for its fourth-quarter cuts.

Despite those pressures, the bank forecasts average return on equity of 16.1% in 2027, up 0.8 percentage points, helped by loan repricing, excess capital and efficiency efforts.

Among Canadian banks, TD Bank remains Bank of America's top pick for its execution and scope for internal improvements, while CIBC stands out for its exposure to domestic investment.

Bank of America expects TD Bank and Royal Bank of Canada (TSX:RY) to reframe their return targets, while Bank of Montreal is expected to reiterate its 15% target for the end of fiscal year 2027.

The next tests of management's plans to improve returns include National Bank of Canada (TSX:NA) strategic update and CIBC's investor day.

Nutanix Inc (NASDAQ:NTNX) lost its "buy" rating at Bank of America, which downgraded the stock to "neutral" and cut its price target to $62 from $78, citing uncertainty over CEO succession.

CEO Rajiv Ramaswami plans to step down once a successor is appointed, and the bank cited strategy and execution risks in lowering its valuation multiple from six times estimated 2027 calendar-year sales to four times estimated 2028 sales.

Bank of America also revised its estimates following updated guidance from Nutanix, which expects its roughly 5-percentage-point first-quarter margin beat to provide little benefit over the rest of fiscal 2027.

Planned hiring and spending on AI, cloud-native products and data sovereignty offerings limit those gains, and the bank said the scale of investment needed to compete in AI remains unclear.

Learn more about Nutanix

Read more about Nutanix

Those spending plans come amid weaker customer metrics, with net revenue retention slipping to 105% and calculated bookings tied to remaining performance obligations falling about 2% year over year.

Fewer large deals closed, and the bank saw limited evidence that the company was fully benefiting from strong sales of standard servers, even though its revenue is tied to enterprise server core counts.

Bank of America sees external storage as Nutanix's clearest near-term growth opportunity, citing the quarter's largest deal using Dell Technologies Inc (NASDAQ:DELL) PowerFlex and the broader availability of NetApp support.

Support for existing storage arrays also helps customers migrate from VMware, which the bank sees as a longer-term opportunity, while a prolonged CEO search poses a more immediate risk.

Bank of America Corporation BAC is strengthening its international banking franchise through significant expansion in Switzerland, where it recently marked 75 years of operations. The bank's Swiss corporate banking client base has tripled since January 2024, with client numbers increasing nearly 30% year to date. Further, since the launch of its Swiss growth initiative in 2021, the local workforce has doubled, reflecting continued investments in its international business.

Bank of America is expanding its Swiss operations by strengthening Financial Institutions Group (FIG) coverage, broadening corporate banking capabilities and growing its middle-market offering. The bank's local business spans mergers and acquisitions (M&A) advisory, equity and debt capital markets, corporate banking and Global Markets.

BAC has advised on several significant transactions involving Swiss companies over the past 18 months, including deals involving Lonza, ABB, Nestlé, Galderma, DocMorris and Swisscom. The bank has also strengthened its capital markets presence by underwriting equity and debt offerings, including Galderma's secondary accelerated bookbuild and bond offerings for Swisscom, Nestlé and Novartis.

The expansion aligns with Bank of America's broader international middle-market strategy, which initially gained traction in Switzerland and has since expanded into the United Kingdom, Ireland, Italy and Germany. The initiative provides companies with access to financing, treasury, payments and foreign exchange solutions, strengthening the bank's ability to serve businesses across multiple markets. Continued investments in local teams and broader client coverage should help deepen corporate relationships, generate cross-border business opportunities and diversify revenue streams.

BAC's investment banking fees increased 14.6% year over year in the first nine months of 2026, reflecting a recovery in capital markets activity. Although third-quarter investment banking fees, excluding self-led deals, declined 11% year over year, the bank remains focused on strengthening its advisory and capital markets capabilities. Continued international expansion and a growing corporate client base could support future advisory mandates, financing transactions and fee income generation.

Over the past three months, shares of BAC have declined 20.6%, underperforming the industry's 15.4% decline.
